'''''Cucumis anguria''''', commonly known as '''maroon cucumber''',<ref name="fao">{{cite web|url=http://ecocrop.fao.org/ecocrop/srv/en/cropView?id=5008|title=''Cucumis anguria''|date=1993–2007|work=EcoCrop|publisher=[[Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations|FAO]]|accessdate=November 4, 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150702205633/http://ecocrop.fao.org/ecocrop/srv/en/cropView?id=5008|archive-date=July 2, 2015|url-status=dead}}</ref> '''West Indian gherkin''',<ref name=plants>{{ cite web |url=https://plants.usda.gov/java/profile?symbol=CUAN |title=Profile for ''Cucumis anguria'' (West Indian gherkin) |work=PLANTS Database |publisher=USDA, [[Natural Resources Conservation Service|NRCS]] |access-date=November 4, 2012}}</ref> '''maxixe''',<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://worldcrops.org/crops/maxixe|title=Maxixe {{!}} WorldCrops|website=worldcrops.org|access-date=2020-04-26}}</ref> '''burr gherkin''',<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.motherearthnews.com/organic-gardening/growing-burr-gherkins-zmaz08djzgoe|title=Growing Burr Gherkins - Organic Gardening|last=Weaver|first=William Woys|website=Mother Earth News|language=en|access-date=2020-04-26|author-link=William Woys Weaver}}</ref> '''cackrey''',<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://ecocrop.fao.org/ecocrop/srv/en/cropView?id=5008|title=Cackery|last=|first=|date=|website=|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150702205633/http://ecocrop.fao.org/ecocrop/srv/en/cropView?id=5008|archive-date=2015-07-02|access-date=}}</ref> and '''West Indian gourd''',<ref name=fao/> is a [[vine]] that is [[indigenous (ecology)|indigenous]] to [[Africa]], but has become [[naturalisation (biology)|naturalized]] in the [[New World]], and is [[plant cultivation|cultivated]] in many places.<ref name=grin/> It is similar and related to the common [[cucumber]] (''[[Cucumber|C. sativus]]'') and its [[cultivar]]s are known as [[gherkin]]s.{{citation needed|date=November 2012}}

==Description==
''Cucumis anguria'' is a thinly stemmed, herbaceous vine scrambling up to 3 meters long. [[Fruit]]s (4–5 cm × 3–4 cm) grow on long stalks, and are ovoid to oblong. The fruits are covered with long hairs over a surface of spines or wart-like bumps. The inner flesh is pallid to green.<ref name=fao/>

==Distribution==
Although naturalized in many parts of the New World, ''Cucumis anguria'' is indigenous only to Africa, in the following countries: [[Angola]]; [[Botswana]]; the [[Democratic Republic of the Congo]]; [[Malawi]]; [[Mozambique]]; [[Namibia]]; [[South Africa]] ([[KwaZulu-Natal]], [[Limpopo]], [[Mpumalanga]]); [[Eswatini]]; [[Tanzania]]; [[Zambia]]; and [[Zimbabwe]].<ref name=grin/>

''Cucumis anguria'' has become naturalized in: [[Anguilla]]; [[Antigua and Barbuda]]; [[Australia]] ([[Queensland]] and [[Western Australia]]<ref name=FloraBase>{{FloraBase|name=''Cucumis anguria''|id=17340}}</ref>); [[Barbados]]; [[Brazil]]; [[Cayman Islands]]; [[Costa Rica]]; [[Cuba]]; the [[Dominican Republic]]; [[Ecuador]]; [[French Guiana]]; [[Grenada]]; [[Guadeloupe]]; [[Guatemala]]; [[Haiti]]; [[Honduras]]; [[Jamaica]]; [[Madagascar]]; [[Martinique]]; [[Mexico]]; [[Netherlands Antilles]]; [[Nicaragua]]; [[Panama]]; [[Peru]]; [[Puerto Rico]]; [[Saint Lucia]]; [[Saint Vincent and Grenadines]]; [[Suriname]]; the United States ([[California]], [[Florida]], [[Georgia (U.S. state)|Georgia]], [[Massachusetts]], [[Montana]], [[New York (state)|New York]], [[Oregon]], [[Texas]], [[Minnesota]], [[Wisconsin]] and [[Washington (state)|Washington]]); Canada ([[Ontario, Niagara Region]], [[Nova Scotia, Hants County]]); [[Venezuela]]; and both [[British Virgin Islands|British]] and [[American Virgin Islands]].<ref name=grin/><ref name=plants/>

''Cucumis anguria'' is also cultivated, but not indigenous to, nor yet believed to have become naturalized in these places: [[Cape Verde]]; [[Réunion]]; [[Senegal]]; and parts of the [[Caribbean]] not already mentioned above.<ref name=grin/>

==Uses==
''Cucumis anguria'' is primarily grown (as a [[crop]] plant) for its edible fruit, which is used in [[pickling]], as cooked [[vegetable]]s,<ref name=fao/><ref name=jwp>{{ cite book |author=Purseglove, J.W. |title=Tropical Crops Dicotyledons |year=1968 |publisher=Longmans, Green and Co. Ltd  |location=London}}</ref> or eaten raw.<ref name=fao/> The flavor is similar to that of the common cucumber.<ref>{{cite web |title=How to Grow Gherkins |url=http://gardeningjones.com/blog/2013/09/03/how-to-grow-gherkins/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130912212046/http://gardeningjones.com/blog/2013/09/03/how-to-grow-gherkins/ |url-status=usurped |archive-date=September 12, 2013 |website=Gardening Jones |accessdate=26 July 2020 |date=3 September 2013}}</ref> ''C. anguria'' fruits are popular in the [[Northeast Region, Brazil|northeast]] and [[North Region, Brazil|north]] of [[Brazil]], where they are an ingredient in the local version of ''[[cozido]]'' (meat-and-vegetable stew).{{citation needed|date=November 2012}}

''Cucumis anguria'' has been used in [[folk medicine]] to treat ailments of the [[stomach]].<ref name=jad>{{cite web|author=James A. Duke|author-link=James A. Duke|title=''Cucumis anguria'' (CUCURBITACEAE)|publisher=Dr. Duke's Phytochemical and Ethnobotanical Databases|url=https://phytochem.nal.usda.gov/phytochem/ethnoPlants/show/9985|accessdate=December 25, 2017|archive-date=April 13, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190413000830/https://phytochem.nal.usda.gov/phytochem/ethnoPlants/show/9985|url-status=dead}}</ref>

==Pests==
Crops are susceptible to attacks by [[fungi]], [[aphid]]s, and [[cucumber beetle]]s.<ref name=fao/>

==Synonyms==
This species, ''Cucumis anguria'' <small>L.</small>, has a name that other species may share:
*''Cucumis anguria'' <small>Forssk.</small>, a synonym for ''[[Cucumis prophetarum]]''
